Do not use colons.

text:
In late August 1854, a terrible illness fell upon Soho, a crowded and poor district of London. Within three days, more than a hundred people living near Broad Street were dead. Within ten days, about five hundred had died. The illness was cholera, which causes violent vomiting and diarrhea, drains the body of fluid, and can kill a healthy adult in a day or two. Residents fled the area, shops closed, and the streets grew quiet.

At that time, almost every educated person believed cholera spread through "miasma," meaning foul air rising from rotting waste and filthy ground. London smelled dreadful, so the theory seemed sensible. John Snow, a physician living nearby, disagreed. He was a careful, sober man who had made his name by studying anesthesia and giving chloroform to patients, including Queen Victoria during childbirth. Years earlier he had reasoned that cholera must enter the body through the mouth and attack the gut. If it were carried on the air, he argued, it would strike the lungs and the whole body at once. Instead it began in the stomach and bowels, which suggested that people swallowed something. He suspected contaminated water.

Few took him seriously. He had published his idea in 1849 and been largely ignored. The Broad Street outbreak gave him a chance to test it on a small, tightly bounded group of people.

Snow began by walking the neighborhood and asking questions. He obtained the list of deaths from the local registrar and visited the homes of the dead. Everyone in the district drew drinking water from public pumps, shared wells dug into the ground where people lined up with buckets. Snow suspected the pump on Broad Street, so he went door to door, asking families where they got their water.

He then did something that now seems obvious but was unusual then. He made a map. On a street plan of Soho, he drew a small black bar at the address of each death, stacking the bars when more than one person died in a house. When he stepped back, the pattern was plain. The deaths clustered thickly around the pump on Broad Street, and thinned out with distance from it.

Snow knew that a skeptic could object, so he looked for the exceptions, and these proved as persuasive as the clusters. Near the pump stood a workhouse housing about five hundred poor residents, yet only five of them died. Investigating, Snow learned that the workhouse had its own well and rarely used the Broad Street pump. A nearby brewery employed seventy workers, and none of them died. The men were given free beer and did not drink from the pump, and the brewery had its own well as well.

There were stranger cases too. A woman in Hampstead, far from Soho, died of cholera. Snow learned that she had once lived in the neighborhood and liked the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had a bottle carried to her every day. Her niece, who drank from the same bottle, also fell ill and died. Neither had been anywhere near the outbreak. Only the water connected them to it.

On September 7, Snow brought his evidence to the local Board of Guardians. The officials were unconvinced of his theory, but the data was striking enough that they agreed to act. The next day, the handle of the Broad Street pump was removed, and the pump could no longer be used.

The outbreak was already fading by then. Many residents had fled, and deaths had been falling for several days, so critics later argued that removing the handle changed little. Snow himself acknowledged that the epidemic might have ended anyway. But the story did not end there.

The missing piece came from the Reverend Henry Whitehead, a local curate who doubted Snow's idea and set out to disprove it. He knew the community well and interviewed residents more thoroughly than Snow could. Instead of refuting the theory, he found the source. An infant had died of cholera in a house at 40 Broad Street shortly before the outbreak, and her mother had washed the baby's soiled diapers and emptied the water into a cesspool only a few feet from the well. Inspection showed the cesspool's brickwork was decayed and leaking into the water supply. Whitehead, once a skeptic, became one of Snow's allies.

Official bodies still rejected the waterborne theory for years, clinging to miasma. Snow died in 1858 at the age of forty-five, without seeing his view accepted. Only later, as germ theory developed, did the world understand what he had shown. Today he is remembered as a founder of epidemiology, the study of how disease spreads through populations. His method was simple and durable. He gathered the facts, mapped them, and followed the evidence even when the experts disagreed.
